overview.intro: This module outlines the five-step pipeline that extracts a heart rate from facial video and previews how video compression corrupts the signal.

read: No chart here. Each heartbeat pumps blood that alters facial skin colour by roughly 0.1 percent, which is invisible to human eyes.
rPPG, or remote photoplethysmography, means reading a pulse from camera video by catching these blood-volume changes in the pixels.
Horizontal axis is time in seconds. Red, green, and blue lines show the average brightness over time across a tracked face box for each colour channel.
Look for the green line carrying the clearest wave, because blood absorbs green light most strongly.
Horizontal axis is time in seconds. The solid orange line is the video pulse extracted by POS, while the dashed grey line is the true pulse from a contact finger sensor.
Look for the orange curve aligning with the grey truth once POS combines the colour channels to cancel shared brightness changes from room lighting.
Horizontal axis is heart rate in bpm (beats per minute); vertical axis is relative power, showing how strongly the signal wiggles at each speed. The orange line is the spectrum.
The search is restricted to the human range of 42 to 180 bpm; look for the tallest peak, which gives the estimated heart rate.
No chart here. Video codecs shrink file sizes for streaming by discarding colour detail the eye will not miss.
Notice how an encoder setting can change the error from 3 bpm to 27 bpm at the same bitrate.

overview.takeaway: A camera can read a pulse from subtle skin colour shifts, but video compression can drown or distort that tiny signal.

waves.intro: This module explains the basic properties of waves and shows that a pulse is a repeating wave.

read: Horizontal axis is time in seconds; vertical axis is wave height. The solid orange line is a pure sine wave, like a pendulum swinging smoothly back and forth.
Use the sliders to adjust frequency in bpm (beats per minute; frequency in Hz means cycles per second, and bpm equals Hz times 60), amplitude (wave height), and phase (horizontal shift).
Horizontal axis is time in seconds. Faint lines show two individual waves, while the thick black line shows their combined sum.
Check the box to add the second wave and adjust its knobs; the sum is a more complex pattern, yet both original waves are still in it.

sections.for: 3. The real pulse is a wave too
read: Horizontal axis is time in seconds; vertical axis is sensor amplitude. The solid grey line is the pulse recorded by a contact finger sensor, with tick marks highlighting wave peaks.
Drag the window slider to inspect different beats; the spacing between peaks gives the heart rate.

waves.takeaway: A pulse is a repeating wave, and the spacing of its peaks reveals the heart rate.

sampling.intro: This module shows how taking periodic camera snapshots captures a continuous wave, and why normal video frame rates do not cause heart-rate aliasing.

read: Horizontal axis is time in seconds; vertical axis is amplitude. The grey line is the true wave, blue dots are camera frame snapshots, and the dashed pink line shows the false slower wave that appears when the camera is too slow.

Lower the frame rate (fps, frames per second) or raise the wave frequency until the Nyquist limit, which is half the frame rate, drops below the wave. The dots then pretend to form a slower wave, like wagon wheels turning backward on film.
Horizontal axis is time in seconds; vertical axis is heart rate in bpm. The grey line is truth from a contact sensor, while the orange line is the video measurement with frames dropped.

Increase the slider; the estimate stays accurate until the effective frame rate drops near 6 fps, because the 42 to 180 bpm (0.7 to 3 Hz) heart-rate band sits well below the 15 Hz Nyquist limit of 30 fps video.

sampling.takeaway: Standard camera frame rates are far too fast to cause aliasing on human heart rates, so compression failures come from something else.

fourier.intro: This module shows how the Fourier transform splits a noisy signal into pure frequencies, giving a spectrum.

sections.for: 1. From a messy trace to its ingredients
read: Top chart shows the noisy signal over time; bottom chart shows its spectrum, plotting power versus frequency in bpm, with the 42 to 180 bpm heart-rate band shaded green.

The spectrum acts like an ear separating the notes in a chord. Move the tone sliders to see peaks shift, and raise the noise to see that random noise makes a flat floor while steady tones form sharp spikes.
Horizontal axis is frequency in bpm; vertical axis is relative power. Black dashed lines mark the true positions of the two tones.
Lengthen the window slider; resolution is about 60 divided by window seconds, in bpm, so a short window merges close tones into one mound while a longer window shows two peaks.

sections.for: 3. Why the window is faded at its edges
read: Horizontal axis is frequency in bpm; vertical axis is power in decibels (dB, where each minus 10 dB means ten times weaker). The grey line is an un-tapered window and the orange line uses a Hann taper.
Compare the lines away from the centre peak. Cutting a signal abruptly creates leakage, a skirt of false frequencies; the Hann taper fades the window ends smoothly and suppresses it.

fourier.takeaway: The Fourier transform picks a periodic pulse out of noise, provided the window is long enough and tapered at its ends.

filter.intro: This module shows how filtering removes unwanted frequencies from a skin colour trace, and why non-sine repeating shapes produce a comb of harmonics.

sections.for: 1. A band-pass filter on the real trace
read: Top chart shows the spectrum in decibels (dB) versus bpm, with the passband shaded green. Lower charts show the raw and filtered signals over time and the filtered signal against the contact sensor.

A band-pass filter acts like stereo tone controls, keeping 0.7 to 3 Hz (42 to 180 bpm) while cutting drift from posture and light. Try No filtering to see the median error jump from 0.5 bpm to about 108 bpm.

sections.for: 2. A repeating shape is a family of waves
read: Top chart shows the repeating waveform; bottom chart shows its spectrum with vertical markers at multiples of the repetition rate and the green heart-rate band shaded.
Switch from sine to sawtooth; sharp repeating jumps produce harmonics (extra frequencies at whole multiples, like overtones on a guitar string), a comb of false peaks inside the heart-rate band.

filter.takeaway: A band-pass filter removes slow drift, but harmonics of repeating jumps sit inside the allowed band and pass straight through.

skin.intro: This module shows that each heartbeat subtly changes facial skin colour and maps which face areas carry the strongest pulse.

read: Left video shows the original cropped footage; right video shows the subtle colour fluctuation amplified by software.
Play the videos; the pulse shifts brightness by only about 0.1 percent, which camera noise hides on single pixels but averaging reveals.

sections.for: 2. Where on the face is the pulse?
read: Left panel is a face tile grid where darker tiles correlate more with the contact sensor; right chart shows the selected tile's green brightness against the contact truth.
Click different tiles; skin tiles tend to follow the true pulse, whereas hair, clothing and edge tiles contain mostly noise.

skin.takeaway: Blood absorbs green light to create a faint colour pulse that shows only when many pixels are averaged.

trace.intro: This module shows how averaging thousands of facial pixels produces red, green and blue colour traces over time.

read: Left video shows the face region box. Right chart shows channel brightness in red, green and blue over time, with the contact sensor as truth.
Toggle between raw drift and pulse band only; the raw trace wanders with lighting, but band-pass filtering reveals the pulse, which is largest in green.
Horizontal axis is time in seconds; vertical axis is relative brightness. The green line is the average of k skin tiles; the dashed grey line is the contact sensor.
Drag the tiles slider from 1 upward; single tiles are ragged, but averaging cancels independent noise so the shared pulse emerges.

trace.takeaway: Averaging many pixels removes camera noise and leaves a colour trace where the heartbeat shows, most clearly in green.

pos.intro: This module explains POS, a short algebraic recipe that combines colour channels to cancel lighting changes without machine learning.

read: Horizontal axis is time in seconds; vertical axis is pixel value. Red, green and blue lines show the raw windowed averages.
The tiny heartbeat wiggles are invisible at this scale.

sections.for: Divide each channel by its own average
read: Lines show each channel divided by its window average, so all hover near 1.0.
This puts the channels on the same scale, so a lighting shift moves all of them together while blood flow moves them differently.

sections.for: Project onto two directions that cancel brightness
read: The two lines are projections whose channel weights sum to zero.
Opposing weights cancel uniform brightness shifts, leaving the colour changes that differ between channels.

sections.for: Mix the two with a weight so noise cancels
read: The combined signal h is built from the two projections with a weight alpha.
The weight balances the projections so the leftover non-pulse noise cancels.

sections.for: Slide the window one frame at a time and add the results
read: The orange line is the POS pulse; dashed grey is the contact sensor truth.
Overlap-add slides the window and sums the results, which smooths over errors in any single window.

sections.for: Why does this beat "just use green"?
read: Axes show time and heart rate under added artificial lighting flicker.
Raise the flicker strength; green-only misreads flicker as pulse, but POS cancels it because flicker moves all channels together.

pos.takeaway: POS extracts a clean pulse by combining colour channels so that shared lighting shifts cancel out.

hr.intro: This module shows how the pulse signal becomes beats per minute: take a 10-second window and find the dominant frequency in its spectrum.

read: Both graphs show the same 10 s slice. The top graph plots the pulse signal against time in seconds; the orange line is the video pulse, the purple line is the same slice after the Hann taper, and the dotted grey curve is the taper shape.
Use the window slider to inspect different segments. The Hann taper fades the window edges to zero so artificial edge jumps do not distort the frequency analysis.
The bottom graph plots signal strength against speed in bpm; height shows how much of the signal wiggles at that speed. Orange is the video pulse and dashed grey is the contact sensor truth.

Like picking out the notes in a piano chord, the spectrum separates speeds. The tall hump marks the heart rate, and orange overlapping grey means the camera is right. Coarse or Fine only changes how finely the axis is sampled.
Horizontal axis is time in seconds across the recording; vertical axis is heart rate in bpm. Orange is the video estimate and grey is the contact sensor truth.
Compare the two curves; close agreement means uncompressed video measures the heart rate reliably.

hr.takeaway: The tallest peak in a 10-second window's spectrum gives the heart rate.

codec.intro: This module shows how compression discards subtle colour detail and varies picture quality frame by frame to stay on a bitrate budget.

read: Each strip shows one encode; coloured ticks mark keyframes (I-frames, stored as whole pictures). Frames between ticks are P-frames, which store only what changed.
Compare the spacing of ticks (the GOP size); frequent keyframes help video calls recover from lost packets but make a regular repeating pattern.

sections.for: 2. The quantiser: how coarsely each frame is rounded
read: Horizontal axis is time in seconds; vertical axis is mean QP (quantiser). The line tracks how coarsely each frame is rounded, with dotted lines marking keyframes.
A higher QP rounds more coarsely, saving bits. Look for QP moving with the keyframe cycle.
Left video shows the decoded output; right video shows its brightness difference from the original, amplified 12 times, where mid-grey means no error.
Pixel errors look like random noise that cancels when averaged over the face; a whole-face brightness shift from the keyframe cycle does not cancel.

sections.for: 4. How much does it hurt the heart rate?
read: Bars show median error in bpm across 42 subjects at bitrates from 1600 kbps down to 100 kbps, with a single keyframe; whiskers span the middle half of windows.
Error stays small at 800 kbps and above and grows sharply below 400 kbps as coarse rounding erases the faint colour change.

codec.takeaway: Compression rounds away the subtle skin flush and makes picture quality swing with the keyframe cycle.

keyframe.intro: This module walks step by step through why regular keyframes make the heart-rate estimate lock onto false values.

sections.for: 1. Two encodes of one video. Can you see a difference?
read: Side-by-side videos of the same footage at the same bitrate: one with a single keyframe, one with keyframes at a fixed spacing.
They look the same to the eye, yet the heart-rate error jumps from about 3 bpm to about 27 bpm.

sections.for: 2. At every keyframe the face colour jumps, then drifts
read: Top chart plots the face green error over time with markers at keyframes; the second chart folds all cycles on top of each other and averages them.
Brightness jumps at each keyframe and drifts back afterwards, a sawtooth about as large as the pulse itself.

sections.for: 3. A repeating jump contains a whole family of frequencies
read: The chart shows the spectrum of the colour error with dashed lines at the harmonic teeth.
A jump repeating every T seconds has harmonics at multiples of 60/T bpm, a comb of peaks inside the 42 to 180 bpm heart-rate band.

sections.for: 4. The algorithm picks the loudest tooth
read: Horizontal axis is heart rate in bpm; the coloured line is the compressed spectrum, grey the uncompressed one, black dashed the truth.
The estimator reports the tallest peak in the band, so when a tooth is taller than the true pulse it reports the tooth.

sections.for: 5. Over the whole minute, the answer snaps to a tooth
read: Horizontal axis is time in seconds; vertical axis is heart rate in bpm. Grey is contact truth; the coloured line is the compressed video estimate.
Watch the estimate leave the true heart rate and sit on horizontal lines that mark the harmonic teeth.

sections.for: 6. Move the keyframes and the false peak moves with them
read: Choose a keyframe spacing and see where the false peaks land across subjects.
When the spacing changes, the teeth and the errors move with it, which ties the failure to the encoder's keyframe timing.

sections.for: 7. The decoder knows where the keyframes are. Can it undo the pattern?
read: The chart compares the spectrum before and after subtracting a fitted repeating pattern; bars compare median errors.
Subtracting the pattern roughly halves the error but does not reach the pre-set bar of within 2 bpm of single-keyframe error.
Bars show the median heart-rate error across 42 subjects at 800 kbps for different keyframe settings.
At the same bitrate, regular keyframes raise the median error many times over compared with a single keyframe.

Below it, the deep-network panel compares POS, CHROM, TS-CAN and PhysNet: pale bar = error with one keyframe, solid bar = error with regular keyframes. A big jump means the method was fooled. Change the bitrate and spacing with the buttons.

keyframe.takeaway: Regular keyframes create a repeating brightness sawtooth whose harmonics pose as heartbeats and derail the estimate.

results.intro: This module summarises which questions the experiments answered, which came back empty, and what remains open.

read: The table lists each question, the evidence, and the outcome.

Compression damage and keyframe locking are confirmed, the decoder-side fix is partial, deep networks are mostly not fooled (TS-CAN at 800 kbps) but break at 400 kbps with 1 s keyframes, and the QP reliability signal came back empty.

sections.for: Why the "free reliability signal" came back empty
read: Horizontal axis is the share of windows kept; vertical axis is mean error in bpm. The curves compare an ideal ranking, the QP gate, a bitrate-only baseline and random.
QP tracks bitrate closely across streams (correlation 0.92), but within one stream it varies by only about 0.6 QP, so it adds little.

sections.for: What would settle the open questions
read: The table lists the future experiments that would resolve the open questions.
Subjects here sat still, so moving and speaking faces remain untested.

results.takeaway: Keyframe spacing disrupts rPPG more than bitrate alone, while encoder QP gave no useful reliability signal on still subjects.

lab.intro: This lab lets you combine any subject, encode and algorithm and see the pulse, spectrum and whole-minute track together.

read: Horizontal axis is time in seconds. The coloured line is the extracted pulse; dashed grey is the contact sensor.
Change subject and encode and compare how closely the coloured wave follows the grey one.
Horizontal axis is heart rate in bpm; vertical axis is relative power. The coloured line is the compressed spectrum; other lines mark the truth and harmonic teeth.
Look for teeth that rise above the true pulse peak in keyframe encodes.
Horizontal axis is time in seconds; vertical axis is heart rate in bpm. The coloured line is the video estimate and grey is the contact truth.
Check whether the estimate follows the grey line or snaps onto horizontal tooth lines, and read the median error.

lab.takeaway: Changing the encode and algorithm shows directly how compression settings change the waveform, spectrum and heart-rate track.

quant.intro: This module turns the QP dial on a real frame of the recording and shows what it removes, how small the file gets, and the point where the pulse is lost.

read: QP (quantiser parameter, 0 to 51) is how coarsely the encoder stores the picture: low = fine and big, high = rough and small. Three pictures: the original, the encoded frame, and their difference multiplied up by the gain (grey = no change).
Click a QP button; click any picture to pick the 8×8 square inspected below. Watch the bitrate fall and the difference picture fill with texture loss and block edges.

sections.for: 2. What "round more coarsely" means: one block of pixels
read: The encoder rewrites each block as 64 ingredients (flat brightness, gradients, fine texture), then rounds each ingredient to a multiple of the step size. Ingredients that round to zero cost nothing to store.

Left: original block. Middle: the rounded ingredients (· = zero). Right: the rebuilt block. Raise QP and watch ingredients vanish and the pixel error grow. This is a simplified teaching coder, not H.264 itself.

sections.for: 3. Does the pulse survive? Heart-rate error at each QP
read: Left chart: the video pulse (orange) against the contact sensor (grey) in one 10 s window, both scaled to the same size. Right chart: the heart-rate estimate over the minute against the truth. Bars: median error per QP.
Step the QP up until the orange wave stops following the grey one; the bars show the cliff.
Original and one encode played in sync. Pause and compare skin texture; the pulse itself is not visible to the eye in either.

quant.takeaway: QP decides how much fine detail the encoder keeps; the faint pulse is far below the step size, so once QP passes a threshold the heart rate is lost even though the picture still looks fine.
